articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M tourism contract renewal skipped competitive bidding. Commissioners say that's fine.
articles.dek: The deal with Visit Pensacola went through on consent agenda in April. Three months later, no one can explain why procurement rules didn't apply.
brief: Escambia County renewed its $2.3 million annual contract with Visit Pensacola in April without competitive bidding
County procurement policy requires competitive solicitation for contracts over $50,000, but tourism promotion has been treated as exempt since 2019
Commissioners approved the renewal on consent agenda with no discussion; staff could not cite specific legal authority for the exemption
articles.body:
The agenda item took eleven seconds.

On April 18, Escambia County commissioners voted to renew a $2.3 million contract with Visit Pensacola, the nonprofit that markets the county as a tourist destination. The vote happened during the consent agenda—a batch of items approved all at once, no discussion. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh moved to approve. Commissioner Mike Kohler seconded. The gavel came down before anyone could draw a breath to speak.

Three months later, The Flightline asked a straightforward question: Why didn't this contract go through competitive bidding?

No one at the county could provide a clear answer.

The Policy Says One Thing

Escambia County's procurement policy is explicit. Any contract for goods or services exceeding $50,000 requires competitive solicitation—either sealed bids or a request for proposals. The policy, last updated in 2023, makes limited exceptions: emergencies, sole-source purchases where only one vendor exists, and contracts with other government entities.

Visit Pensacola is none of these things. It's a 501(c)(6) nonprofit with a board of directors drawn from local hoteliers, restaurateurs and tourism operators. It has competitors. Destinations International, the tourism industry's trade association, lists more than a dozen destination marketing firms that work with Florida counties.

Yet when The Flightline requested documentation showing why competitive bidding didn't apply, county staff initially said they would need to research the question.

A week later, County Administrator Wes Moreno's office provided a two-sentence response: "The Visit Pensacola contract has historically been treated as a tourism development partnership rather than a standard procurement. This arrangement predates current procurement policy."

The response did not cite any specific ordinance, resolution or legal opinion.

How We Got Here

Visit Pensacola's relationship with the county dates to 2019, when commissioners dissolved the old Pensacola Bay Area Convention and Visitors Bureau and contracted with the newly formed nonprofit instead. That original contract was also approved without competitive bidding. Meeting minutes from November 2019 show then-County Administrator Amy Lovoy describing the arrangement as a "public-private partnership" that didn't require standard procurement.

No commissioner asked for a legal opinion at the time. None has asked since.

The contract has been renewed three times. Each renewal added money. The original deal was $1.8 million annually. By 2024, it had grown to $2.1 million. This year's renewal bumped it to $2.3 million—funded entirely by the county's share of tourist development tax revenue, the so-called bed tax collected from hotels and vacation rentals.

Visit Pensacola's CEO, Darien Schaefer, declined an interview request. A spokesperson for the organization provided a written statement: "Visit Pensacola has proudly served as Escambia County's destination marketing organization for seven years. We are focused on driving tourism and economic impact for our community."

The statement did not address the procurement question.

What Competitive Bidding Would Look Like

Other Florida counties treat destination marketing differently.

In 2022, Hillsborough County issued a request for proposals when its tourism contract came up for renewal. Four firms responded. Visit Tampa Bay, the incumbent, won the contract—but only after demonstrating its value against competitors.

Leon County did the same in 2021. So did Bay County in 2023, following its post-Hurricane Michael tourism recovery.

"It's just good governance," said Patricia Morrow, a procurement specialist who consults with Florida municipalities. "When you're spending public money at this scale, you want to know you're getting the best value. The only way to know that is to let the market tell you."

Morrow reviewed Escambia County's procurement policy at The Flightline's request. She found no language that would exempt tourism contracts.

"If they have a legal justification, they should be able to produce it," she said. "The fact that they can't is concerning."

The Commissioners' View

The Flightline contacted all five county commissioners. Two responded.

Commissioner Steven Barry, whose District 5 includes Pensacola Beach, said he was satisfied with Visit Pensacola's performance and saw no reason to change the arrangement.

"They've done a good job marketing the destination," Barry said. "Hotel occupancy is up. Bed tax revenue is up. Why would we rock the boat?"

Asked whether the county should at least verify through competitive bidding that it's getting the best deal, Barry said: "I trust our staff to make those recommendations. If there was a problem, they'd bring it to us."

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 includes much of Pensacola's urban core, said he was not aware that competitive bidding had been bypassed.

"I'll have to look into that," May said. "I assumed this went through the normal process."

May did not respond to follow-up questions.

Commissioners Bergosh, Kohler and Doug Underhill did not return calls or emails.

Performance Questions

The absence of competitive bidding raises a secondary question: How does the county evaluate whether Visit Pensacola is doing its job?

The contract requires quarterly reports on "marketing activities and tourism metrics." The Flightline obtained the four most recent reports through a public records request.

The reports are heavy on activity—advertising campaigns launched, trade shows attended, social media impressions generated. They are light on outcomes. Hotel occupancy rates are cited but not compared to competing destinations or national trends. Return on investment is mentioned but never calculated.

The contract does not include performance benchmarks. There are no penalties for underperformance. The county has no formal process for determining whether $2.3 million in annual spending is producing $2.3 million in value.

"That's a lot of money to spend on faith," Morrow said.

What Happens Next

The current contract runs through September 2027. That means commissioners will face another renewal decision in roughly fifteen months.

At a June 6 commission meeting, local resident Walter Bocchino raised the issue during public comment. He asked commissioners to consider competitive bidding for the next renewal.

"I'm not saying Visit Pensacola is doing a bad job," Bocchino said. "I'm saying we have no way of knowing if someone else could do better for less."

No commissioner responded. The meeting moved to the next agenda item.

The Flightline has submitted a formal public records request for all internal communications regarding the Visit Pensacola contract exemption from procurement rules. The county has 30 days to respond.

This story will be updated as new information becomes available.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: The Cordova Park drainage project is two years behind schedule. Residents are tired of sandbagging.
articles.dek: City engineers blame supply chain delays and redesigns. Homeowners on Bayou Boulevard say they've heard that before—usually right before hurricane season.
brief: The $14.2 million Cordova Park drainage improvement project, originally scheduled for completion in summer 2024, now carries a projected finish date of late 2026
City officials cite pandemic-era supply chain disruptions and two major design revisions as primary causes for the delay
Residents in the flood-prone neighborhood have experienced three significant flooding events since the project broke ground in 2022
articles.body:
The sandbags stacked along Patricia Hendricks' garage door have been there so long they've started to rot. She replaces them twice a year now. Once before hurricane season. Once after.

"I've got a system," Hendricks said, standing in her driveway on Bayou Boulevard last Tuesday. Behind her, a city contractor's truck sat idle at the end of the block. It had been parked there for three days. "The system is: I don't trust anyone else's system."

The Cordova Park Drainage Improvement Project was supposed to fix this. Announced in 2021, funded in 2022, and originally scheduled for completion by August 2024, the $14.2 million infrastructure overhaul promised to address chronic flooding in one of Pensacola's most flood-prone residential areas. Four years later, the project sits at roughly 60 percent completion. The new target date is November 2026. Residents have heard that before.

What the city says happened

According to documents obtained through a public records request, the project has undergone two significant design revisions since breaking ground. The first came in March 2023, when engineers discovered that existing stormwater pipes beneath Bayou Boulevard were in worse condition than initial surveys indicated. The city had to redesign the connection points. That added four months.

The second revision came in January 2024. Supply chain delays on specialized drainage grates—the kind rated for hurricane-force water flow—pushed delivery out by seven months. Rather than wait, city engineers opted to redesign portions of the system to accommodate alternative materials. That redesign took five months. The alternative materials took another three to arrive.

"This project has faced challenges that were frankly unforeseeable when we began," said Marcus Chen, Pensacola's director of public works, at a City Council meeting in April. "We are committed to getting it right, even if that means getting it later than we hoped."

The council accepted his update without comment. No one from Cordova Park spoke during the public forum that night. By then, most had stopped coming.

What residents have lived through

Since construction began in September 2022, homes along Bayou Boulevard and the surrounding streets have flooded three times. Tropical Storm Elise in October 2023 put eight inches of water in Margaret Odom's living room. She's 74. She pulled up her own carpet.

"They told us the construction might make things worse before it got better," Odom said. "They didn't say how much worse. They didn't say how much longer."

The flooding pattern in Cordova Park is well documented. The neighborhood sits in a natural low point between two drainage basins. When heavy rain falls—anything over two inches in an hour—water from the surrounding area funnels toward the bayou that gives the boulevard its name. The existing drainage infrastructure, much of it installed in the 1960s, can't keep up.

The improvement project was designed to increase drainage capacity by roughly 40 percent. It would replace aging pipes, add new catch basins, and install a pump station to move water toward Bayou Texar during surge events. On paper, it would take Cordova Park from a neighborhood that floods routinely to one that floods rarely.

On paper.

The money question

The original project budget was $11.8 million, funded through a combination of municipal bonds and state resilience grants. The current budget stands at $14.2 million. City officials say the increase reflects the design revisions and material cost inflation, not scope creep.

But the funding mechanism creates its own pressure. The state resilience grant—$4.3 million—came with a completion deadline of December 2025. That deadline has now passed. According to Chen's April report, the city applied for and received a one-year extension. If the project isn't substantially complete by December 2026, Pensacola may have to return a portion of those funds.

"Substantially complete" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. City documents define it as "functional infrastructure capable of performing its intended purpose, even if final aesthetic or minor elements remain." In practice, that could mean a working drainage system with unpaved shoulders and temporary fencing. It could mean something less.

Asked for clarification, a city spokesperson said the definition would be determined "in consultation with state officials as the deadline approaches."

What happens now

Construction resumed on the Bayou Boulevard section in early June. Contractors are currently installing the new catch basins that were redesigned last year. The pump station foundation has been poured. The pumps themselves are scheduled to arrive in August.

Scheduled.

Hurricane season started June 1. The National Weather Service's updated forecast, released last month, predicts an above-average season for the Gulf Coast. Pensacola hasn't taken a direct hit from a major hurricane since 2020, but near-misses in 2023 and 2024 caused significant flooding in low-lying areas.

Cordova Park is a low-lying area.

Hendricks, the woman with the rotting sandbags, said she's not counting on the project being done before something bad happens. She's just hoping it gets done at all.

"Every time they push it back, I think about what my house would be worth if I tried to sell it tomorrow," she said. "Then I think about where I'd go. Then I go buy more sandbags."

She gestured toward the idle contractor's truck.

"They'll be back. They always come back. They just never seem to finish."

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and a question: Who's paying for the traffic?
articles.dek: NAS Pensacola's July show generates millions for local businesses. Escambia County picks up the tab for road closures, extra deputies, and beach cleanup.
brief: The annual Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show draws an estimated 200,000 visitors to NAS Pensacola each July, generating significant revenue for hotels, restaurants, and retailers across the metro area.
Escambia County bears the majority of ancillary costs including traffic control, additional law enforcement, emergency services staging, and post-event cleanup on Pensacola Beach.
County commissioners are weighing whether to formalize a cost-sharing agreement with the Navy or establish a dedicated events fund to cover recurring expenses.
articles.body:
The line for the Waffle House on Navy Boulevard starts forming around 5:30 a.m. on air show Saturday. By 6:15, it snakes past the gas pumps next door. Families in lawn chairs. Teenagers in aviator sunglasses. Grandparents who remember when the Blues flew Phantoms.

They've driven from Mobile and Montgomery and Memphis. Some from much farther. They'll spend money at that Waffle House and at the Hampton Inn and at the souvenir shops along Palafox and at the seafood restaurants on Pensacola Beach. Millions of dollars over three days, flowing into cash registers across two counties.

The bill for managing all of it lands somewhere else entirely.

The visible costs

Escambia County Sheriff's Office deployed 47 additional deputies during the 2025 Homecoming Air Show, according to records obtained by The Flightline through a public records request. Overtime costs exceeded $180,000. Traffic control along Blue Angel Parkway and Navy Boulevard required another $34,000 in contracted services.

Pensacola Beach saw its own surge. The Santa Rosa Island Authority reported 12,000 vehicles crossing the Bob Sikes Bridge on air show Saturday alone—more than double a typical July weekend. Escambia County Public Works crews logged 340 hours of post-event cleanup on the beach, where spectators gathered to watch the show from the sand.

"We're not complaining," said County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh during a budget workshop earlier this month. "But we should probably be honest about what this costs us."

The total direct cost to Escambia County for the 2025 show: approximately $412,000, according to figures compiled by the county administrator's office. That doesn't include wear on roads, strain on water and sewer infrastructure, or the opportunity cost of deputies pulled from regular patrols.

The money coming in

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, estimates the Homecoming Air Show generates between $25 million and $32 million in direct visitor spending annually. Hotel occupancy rates top 94% across the metro area during air show weekend. Some properties book out a year in advance.

The economic impact is real. It's also diffuse. Hotel taxes flow to the Tourist Development Council. Sales taxes flow to the state, with a portion returning to local governments months later. The restaurant owner on Palafox sees the benefit immediately. The county budget office sees the cost immediately too.

"There's a timing mismatch," said County Administrator Wes Moreno. "We spend the money in July. We might see some of that return in property taxes the following October, or in sales tax revenue that trickles back over the fiscal year. It's hard to draw a direct line."

The Navy covers costs within the base perimeter. Security, logistics, the show itself—that's federal money. But the moment visitors leave NAS Pensacola's gates, they become the county's responsibility.

A familiar pattern

This isn't unique to the Blue Angels. Pensacola hosts a growing calendar of large events: the Foo Foo Festival, Gallery Night, Bands on the Beach, the Pensacola Marathon. Each generates economic activity. Each requires public services.

The difference is scale. The Homecoming Air Show dwarfs everything else. And unlike a downtown street festival, the impacts spread across the entire metro area—from the hotels near the airport to the beach fifteen miles away.

Commissioner Bergosh has floated the idea of a dedicated events fund, seeded with a portion of tourist development taxes, to cover recurring costs associated with major events. The proposal hasn't gained traction with the full commission.

"It feels like we're subsidizing success," said Commissioner Lumon May at the same budget workshop. "Which maybe we should be. But let's at least acknowledge that's what we're doing."

What the Navy says

Reached for comment, a spokesperson for NAS Pensacola emphasized the base's commitment to community partnership.

"The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show is a source of tremendous pride for the Navy and for Pensacola," the spokesperson said in a written statement. "We work closely with local law enforcement and emergency services to ensure a safe and successful event. We're always open to discussions about how we can continue to strengthen that partnership."

The statement did not address whether the Navy would consider contributing to off-base costs.

Federal installations are generally not permitted to make direct payments to local governments for services rendered outside base boundaries. Any cost-sharing arrangement would likely require creative structuring—perhaps through a nonprofit intermediary or a formal memorandum of understanding.

No such arrangement currently exists.

Looking ahead to July

This year's Homecoming Air Show is scheduled for July 10-11. The Navy expects attendance similar to previous years. Hotels are already booking up.

The Sheriff's Office is planning its deployment. Public Works is scheduling crews. The Tourist Development Council is running ads in Atlanta and New Orleans.

The spectators will come. They'll line Navy Boulevard with coolers and cameras. They'll fill the Waffle House and the Hampton Inn and the restaurants on Pensacola Beach. They'll watch six F/A-18 Super Hornets trace perfect lines across a blue Gulf Coast sky.

And when they leave, someone will sweep up the trash, direct the traffic, and pay the overtime.

The question of who that should be remains, for now, unanswered.
